title_options: Popcorn Jumps On A Leg (Slow Motion Science) 🍿

share.myth: Popcorn just explodes, and the pop is the shell cracking.
share.truth: Kernels burst at about 180 C; foaming starch forms a leg that is compressed on the pan and launches the kernel, and synced video and sound suggest the pop comes from escaping water vapour (Virot & Ponomarenko 2015).
share.line: Popcorn doesn't just burst. It grows a leg of starch, kicks off the pan, and the pop is escaping steam.

facts: Virot E & Ponomarenko A 2015, J R Soc Interface 12:20141247: popcorn bursts, jumps and pops in some hundredths of a second; the critical temperature at which almost all popcorn pops is 180 C, consistent with a pressure-vessel scenario.
Popcorn jumps with a 'leg' of starch that is compressed on the ground; it sits between explosive plants (fracture) and jumping animals (muscles).
Synchronised video and acoustic recordings suggest the 'pop' sound is caused by the release of water vapour. 180 C = 356 F.
description: Slow it down and popcorn does something strange: it grows a leg of starch and jumps off the pan. And the pop isn't the shell cracking. #shorts #science #physics #popcorn
sources: Virot & Ponomarenko 2015, Journal of the Royal Society Interface 12:20141247 (Popcorn: critical temperature, jump and sound), PMC4345489.

scenes.narration: Popcorn doesn't just explode. It jumps, on a leg.
Inside each kernel is a little water, sealed in a hard shell.
Heat it, and that water turns to steam. The pressure inside keeps climbing.
Once it reaches one hundred eighty degrees Celsius, three hundred fifty-six Fahrenheit, almost every kernel bursts.
Starch foams out of the crack, and part of it presses on the pan, like a leg.
The leg squashes, then pushes back, and launches the kernel into the air.
And the pop you hear? Filming and recording it together suggests it's the steam escaping, not the shell cracking.
Popcorn doesn't just burst. It grows a leg of starch, kicks off the pan, and the pop is escaping steam.
So why do some kernels never pop at all?
